questions.stem: A monitor alarm sounds as a CCU patient deteriorates. What is the starting point of the taught response?

choices.text: The routine medication-round sequence
choices.explanation: A new deterioration takes priority over routine sequencing.

choices.text: The previous shift’s stable observations alone
choices.explanation: Earlier stability does not establish the current condition.

choices.text: The patient’s responsiveness, airway, breathing, and circulation
choices.explanation: The monitor is interpreted alongside direct clinical assessment.

choices.text: The monitor’s diagnostic label without patient assessment
choices.explanation: A display does not establish the patient’s current physiological state.

questions.point: Assess the patient and ABCs before relying on the monitor label.

questions.stem: Which observation belongs primarily to the Disability component of the lesson’s rapid assessment?

choices.text: Respiratory effort
choices.explanation: This belongs to Breathing.

choices.text: Pulse and skin perfusion
choices.explanation: These belong to Circulation.

choices.text: Consciousness or new confusion
choices.explanation: Disability includes neurological state.

choices.text: Airway obstruction
choices.explanation: This belongs to Airway.

questions.point: Use focused ABCDE assessment to identify immediate problems.

questions.stem: Which change is a clear deterioration warning in the lesson?

choices.text: New confusion with a marked BP fall
choices.explanation: Both are red flags for impaired perfusion or another acute problem.

choices.text: An unchanged chronic symptom with stable observations
choices.explanation: No acute warning change is described.

choices.text: Pain improving without new symptoms
choices.explanation: This does not identify acute deterioration.

choices.text: Improved breathing with stable BP
choices.explanation: This describes improvement rather than the warning pattern.

questions.point: Recognize sudden clinical red flags.

questions.stem: After an intervention for sudden deterioration, what establishes whether it has helped?

choices.text: The fact that the intervention was prescribed
choices.explanation: A correct order does not establish effectiveness in this patient.

choices.text: The patient’s observations from the previous day alone
choices.explanation: These are not a current post-intervention assessment.

choices.text: The completion of a medication chart entry alone
choices.explanation: Documentation alone does not measure response.

choices.text: Repeat relevant clinical observations and compare the response
choices.explanation: Response must be assessed rather than inferred from treatment being given.

questions.point: Reassess after interventions.

questions.stem: Which focused observation belongs to Exposure in the rapid ABCDE assessment?

choices.text: New confusion and reduced responsiveness
choices.explanation: These primarily assess Disability.

choices.text: Visible bleeding and an abnormal line site
choices.explanation: These are visible potential causes assessed under Exposure.

choices.text: Respiratory effort and breath sounds
choices.explanation: These primarily assess Breathing.

choices.text: The ability to speak through a clear airway
choices.explanation: This primarily assesses Airway.

questions.point: Exposure assessment includes bleeding, lines, edema, and visible causes.

questions.stem: A previously monitored patient is now unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no definite pulse after a prompt check. Which response has priority?

choices.text: Activate the arrest response and begin resuscitation
choices.explanation: Pulseless deterioration requires immediate action.

choices.text: Complete a full medication reconciliation first
choices.explanation: This is secondary to immediate life support.

choices.text: Wait for a laboratory explanation before treating the collapse
choices.explanation: A possible cause does not justify delaying resuscitation.

choices.text: Obtain a routine 12-lead before starting the arrest response
choices.explanation: A diagnostic tracing must not delay resuscitation.

questions.point: Treat a pulseless unresponsive patient as an arrest.

questions.stem: A CCU patient has rapidly worsening dyspnea, falling oxygen saturation, and confusion. Which response best matches the taught sequence?

choices.text: Complete routine discharge education before reassessment
choices.explanation: This delays response to acute instability.

choices.text: Treat the monitor reading without checking breathing or circulation
choices.explanation: Direct patient assessment remains essential.

choices.text: Assess ABCs, obtain current observations, support as indicated, and escalate
choices.explanation: The clinical deterioration requires simultaneous assessment, support, and help.

choices.text: Repeat the previous stable observation values in the chart
choices.explanation: Current findings must be measured and reported.

questions.point: Prepare support while escalating an evolving respiratory/perfusion problem.

questions.stem: VT appears on telemetry. Which current bedside information immediately determines the major treatment pathway?

choices.text: The previous ECG axis and R-wave progression
choices.explanation: Earlier electrical characteristics do not establish current circulation.

choices.text: The last troponin value and planned sampling time
choices.explanation: Biomarkers must not delay current pulse and perfusion assessment.

choices.text: The previous antiarrhythmic dose and its routine due time
choices.explanation: Medication history matters but does not replace the current circulation assessment.

choices.text: Pulse presence and clinical perfusion
choices.explanation: This distinguishes arrest from a stable or unstable pulse-present problem.

questions.point: A dangerous monitor pattern needs immediate patient and pulse correlation.

questions.stem: Which mechanism defines cardiogenic shock in the lesson?

choices.text: An empty intravascular tank as the primary mechanism
choices.explanation: That describes hypovolemic shock.

choices.text: Pathological vasodilation as the primary mechanism
choices.explanation: That describes a distributive pattern.

choices.text: Mechanical obstruction to flow as the primary mechanism
choices.explanation: That describes an obstructive pattern.

choices.text: Insufficient cardiac pumping to perfuse organs
choices.explanation: The primary problem is a weak pump and inadequate effective output.

questions.point: Cardiogenic shock is pump failure with organ hypoperfusion.

questions.stem: Which cluster supports concern about inadequate organ perfusion?

choices.text: A normal pain score with no other findings
choices.explanation: Pain severity does not establish adequate organ perfusion.

choices.text: Cold skin, weak pulses, confusion, and low urine output
choices.explanation: These are taught indicators of hypoperfusion.

choices.text: Warm comfortable skin with stable mentation alone
choices.explanation: This does not establish the low-output cluster.

choices.text: Normal alertness with improving urine output
choices.explanation: This is more consistent with improvement.

questions.point: Recognize a low-perfusion cluster.

questions.stem: Which event most directly provides a pump-failure explanation for shock?

choices.text: A massive pulmonary embolus obstructing forward flow
choices.explanation: This primarily supports an obstructive mechanism.

choices.text: Major gastrointestinal blood loss with reduced circulating volume
choices.explanation: This primarily supports a hypovolemic mechanism.

choices.text: Acute MI with markedly impaired ventricular contraction
choices.explanation: Myocardial injury can reduce output.

choices.text: Severe infection with predominant loss of vascular tone
choices.explanation: This primarily supports a distributive mechanism.

questions.point: MI, severe HF, arrhythmia, and mechanical problems can impair the pump.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches a shock type to its mechanism?

choices.text: Distributive: excessive dilation; obstructive: blocked flow
choices.explanation: These are the taught non-pump mechanisms.

choices.text: Cardiogenic: empty tank; hypovolemic: blocked flow
choices.explanation: This reverses the principal definitions.

choices.text: Hypovolemic: excessive dilation; cardiogenic: blocked flow
choices.explanation: This misidentifies both mechanisms.

choices.text: Distributive: empty tank; obstructive: weak contraction
choices.explanation: Those describe different primary mechanisms.

questions.point: Recognize distributive and obstructive shock mechanisms.

questions.stem: A hypotensive patient has crackles and suspected pump failure. What is the main concern with assuming a large fluid bolus is appropriate?

choices.text: Added fluid reliably distinguishes cardiogenic from hypovolemic shock
choices.explanation: The whole clinical picture must guide the authorized plan.

choices.text: Added fluid directly corrects the loss of myocardial contractility
choices.explanation: Volume is not an inotrope.

choices.text: Added filling load may worsen pulmonary edema
choices.explanation: A failing pump may not handle the extra volume.

choices.text: Added fluid consistently lowers cardiac filling pressure
choices.explanation: This reverses the immediate loading effect.

questions.point: A large automatic fluid bolus may worsen pulmonary edema in pump failure.

questions.stem: Patient A has hypotension, raised JVP, and crackles after MI. Patient B has hypotension after major fluid loss, flat neck veins, and clear lungs. Which comparison fits?

choices.text: A suggests cardiogenic; B suggests hypovolemic shock
choices.explanation: The congestion and volume-loss contexts support different mechanisms.

choices.text: Both are established as distributive solely from low BP
choices.explanation: Hypotension alone does not identify the mechanism.

choices.text: Both are established as obstructive solely from low BP
choices.explanation: The cases do not provide that common mechanism.

choices.text: A suggests hypovolemic; B suggests cardiogenic shock
choices.explanation: This reverses the principal patterns.

questions.point: Differentiate pump failure from volume-loss patterns using the full picture.

questions.stem: During treatment, BP improves but confusion, cool skin, and oliguria persist. Which conclusion is most defensible?

choices.text: Oliguria establishes successful decongestion by itself
choices.explanation: Low output does not establish a beneficial treatment response.

choices.text: Cool skin excludes ongoing shock
choices.explanation: Coolness can be a hypoperfusion sign.

choices.text: The BP improvement establishes complete recovery
choices.explanation: Persistent organ findings contradict that inference.

choices.text: Perfusion remains concerning despite a better BP
choices.explanation: Multiple organ indicators must improve before response is assumed.

questions.point: A BP value must be interpreted with organ perfusion.

questions.stem: Which primary role best describes norepinephrine in this comparison?

choices.text: Increase vascular tone and support pressure
choices.explanation: It is primarily a vasopressor in this lesson.

choices.text: Block the gastric proton pump
choices.explanation: That is an acid-suppression role.

choices.text: Reduce platelet aggregation
choices.explanation: That is an antiplatelet role.

choices.text: Increase renal glucose excretion
choices.explanation: That is an SGLT2-inhibitor role.

questions.point: Norepinephrine primarily supports vascular tone and pressure.

questions.stem: Which primary role best describes dobutamine?

choices.text: Suppress gastric acid through proton-pump blockade
choices.explanation: This is a PPI action.

choices.text: Reduce cardiac contractility through beta1 blockade
choices.explanation: This is the opposite adrenergic action.

choices.text: Inhibit platelet P2Y12 receptors
choices.explanation: This is an antiplatelet action.

choices.text: Increase cardiac contractility and output
choices.explanation: It primarily supports the pump.

questions.point: Dobutamine primarily supports contractility and output.

questions.stem: Which group best evaluates the response and safety of these vasoactive infusions?

choices.text: INR, tablet count, and diet history alone
choices.explanation: These do not establish the immediate infusion response.

choices.text: Wound length, suture count, and joint range alone
choices.explanation: These address another clinical domain.

choices.text: BP, rhythm, perfusion, and urine output
choices.explanation: These follow hemodynamic response and potential adverse effects.

choices.text: Stool color, bowel frequency, and oral lesions alone
choices.explanation: These do not assess the principal hemodynamic effects.

questions.point: Monitor rhythm, pressure, urine output, and peripheral perfusion.

questions.stem: A patient has both inadequate contractility and dangerously low arterial pressure. Why might the team prescribe both medicines?

choices.text: They are identical drugs with different trade names
choices.explanation: They have distinct pharmacological roles.

choices.text: They address different components of the hemodynamic problem
choices.explanation: Dobutamine supports contractility while norepinephrine supports vascular pressure.

choices.text: They both work by inhibiting cardiac beta1 receptors
choices.explanation: Both are not beta1 antagonists.

choices.text: They replace the need to monitor clinical perfusion
choices.explanation: Vasoactive treatment increases the need for monitoring.

questions.point: Pressure and pump support may be combined.

questions.stem: A norepinephrine bag is changed to twice the concentration while the required dose is unchanged. What mL/hour change gives the same drug amount?

choices.text: Half the previous mL/hour
choices.explanation: Doubling concentration halves the volume needed for the same dose.

choices.text: Four times the previous mL/hour
choices.explanation: This would cause a still larger drug delivery increase.

choices.text: Twice the previous mL/hour
choices.explanation: This would deliver four times the prior drug amount.

choices.text: The same mL/hour
choices.explanation: This would double the delivered drug amount.

questions.point: mL/hour depends on the ordered dose and prepared concentration.
Convert a specified infusion dose and concentration into mL/hour.
questions.stem: For an authorized training-case order, the required dose is 4 micrograms/min and the ready infusion concentration is 8 micrograms/mL. What pump rate delivers that dose?
questions.explanation: 4 divided by 8 is 0.5 mL/min; multiply by 60 for 30 mL/hour.

questions.stem: BP improves during peripheral norepinephrine, but the IV site becomes painful, pale, and cool. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: Local pain is evidence that the prescribed dose is too low
choices.explanation: The site change is not a valid reason to increase the infusion.

choices.text: Local pallor establishes that the entire circulating volume has fallen
choices.explanation: The local signs require a site-focused assessment.

choices.text: A local infusion complication can coexist with systemic pressure benefit
choices.explanation: Assess and escalate the threatened site promptly.

choices.text: The BP improvement establishes local tissue safety
choices.explanation: Systemic response does not exclude local ischemia/extravasation.

questions.point: Norepinephrine monitoring includes peripheral IV site ischemia/extravasation signs.

questions.stem: Which ECG pattern is compatible with low potassium in this lesson?

choices.text: A shortened QT as the main calcium pattern
choices.explanation: This relates to a different electrolyte effect.

choices.text: A pacing spike followed by a captured QRS
choices.explanation: This describes pacing rather than potassium status.

choices.text: Independent atrial and ventricular rates alone
choices.explanation: This identifies a conduction relationship, not a specific low-potassium pattern.

choices.text: Flattened T waves or U waves
choices.explanation: These can accompany hypokalemia and ectopy.

questions.point: Low potassium can cause flat T waves/U waves and arrhythmia.

questions.stem: Why is magnesium relevant when hypokalemia is difficult to correct?

choices.text: Normal magnesium eliminates every arrhythmia cause
choices.explanation: Rhythm problems have multiple possible causes.

choices.text: Low magnesium can make potassium correction harder
choices.explanation: The lesson identifies their clinically important relationship.

choices.text: Low magnesium reliably shortens the potassium treatment course
choices.explanation: Deficiency can interfere with correction rather than reliably shorten it.

choices.text: Magnesium directly replaces potassium ion for ion
choices.explanation: They are different electrolytes.

questions.point: Low magnesium can contribute to ventricular arrhythmia and refractory hypokalemia.

questions.stem: Which calcium/QT pairing matches the lesson?

choices.text: Low calcium: longer QT; high calcium: shorter QT
choices.explanation: The direction of the QT effect differs with calcium status.

choices.text: Low calcium: shorter QT; high calcium: longer QT
choices.explanation: This reverses the taught relationship.

choices.text: Low calcium: pacing capture; high calcium: AV dissociation
choices.explanation: Those are not calcium/QT definitions.

choices.text: Low calcium: no QT effect; high calcium: no QT effect
choices.explanation: Calcium influences ventricular repolarization.

questions.point: Calcium affects QT in opposite directions when low or high.

questions.stem: Which potassium administration is specifically prohibited by the lesson?

choices.text: An authorized oral dose when indicated
choices.explanation: Oral treatment is not the rapid-IV-push hazard.

choices.text: A verified protocol-controlled infusion
choices.explanation: Properly prescribed controlled infusion is a different method.

choices.text: Rapid IV push
choices.explanation: Concentrated rapid IV potassium can cause fatal cardiac effects.

choices.text: A prescribed and monitored replacement plan
choices.explanation: The prohibition concerns uncontrolled rapid IV administration.

questions.point: Never give IV potassium as a rapid IV push.

questions.stem: A patient with high potassium develops progressive QRS widening and bradycardia. What does the ECG change indicate?

choices.text: An isolated artifact established by the potassium result
choices.explanation: A known electrolyte problem does not make the ECG change artifact.

choices.text: Potentially dangerous electrical toxicity needing urgent escalation
choices.explanation: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is a time-critical problem.

choices.text: A reliable sign of improved potassium clearance
choices.explanation: Worsening conduction is not evidence of successful correction.

choices.text: An expected therapeutic pacing response
choices.explanation: No pacing intervention is described.

questions.point: Severe high potassium can widen QRS and produce bradyarrhythmia/arrest.

questions.stem: A patient receiving a loop diuretic develops new ventricular ectopy. Which investigation pair best addresses the lesson’s immediate medication/electrolyte link?

choices.text: Amylase and lipase
choices.explanation: These assess a different organ system.

choices.text: Albumin and bilirubin
choices.explanation: These do not best assess the immediate electrolyte-linked rhythm issue.

choices.text: TSH and thyroxine
choices.explanation: Thyroid testing does not best target the acute loop-diuretic loss context.

choices.text: Potassium and magnesium
choices.explanation: Diuretic-associated losses can contribute to ventricular irritability.

questions.point: Loop-diuretic-associated PVCs warrant potassium and magnesium review.

questions.stem: A patient has recurrent torsades de pointes. Which electrolyte is specifically important in the treatment role taught here?

choices.text: Magnesium
choices.explanation: The lesson highlights magnesium in torsades.

choices.text: Sodium
choices.explanation: This is not the specifically highlighted torsades electrolyte.

choices.text: Phosphate
choices.explanation: This is not the specifically highlighted torsades electrolyte.

choices.text: Chloride
choices.explanation: This is not the specifically highlighted torsades electrolyte.

questions.point: Magnesium is important in torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: Which presentation best matches the furosemide role in this lesson?

choices.text: An isolated mechanical bowel obstruction
choices.explanation: This is not the diuretic indication.

choices.text: Isolated low glucose requiring immediate replacement
choices.explanation: Furosemide does not supply glucose.

choices.text: An isolated oral fungal infection
choices.explanation: This requires a different treatment.

choices.text: Breathlessness, crackles, and edema from congestion
choices.explanation: The loop diuretic helps remove excess fluid.

questions.point: Furosemide treats congestion and fluid overload.

sourceRefs.label: Why the patient may receive it

questions.stem: Which effect links furosemide to reduced congestion?

choices.text: Increased platelet aggregation
choices.explanation: This is not the decongestive mechanism.

choices.text: Increased gastric acid secretion
choices.explanation: This does not remove excess fluid.

choices.text: Increased salt and water excretion
choices.explanation: Diuresis reduces excess fluid burden.

choices.text: Reduced ventricular pacing threshold
choices.explanation: This is not the taught mechanism.

questions.point: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that increases urine output.

questions.stem: Which monitoring group is most relevant during furosemide therapy?

choices.text: Tendon pain, supplement cations, and antibacterial susceptibility alone
choices.explanation: These describe a different drug-safety domain.

choices.text: BP, urine output, potassium, renal function, and fluid status
choices.explanation: These follow benefit and important adverse effects.

choices.text: INR, platelet aggregation, and vitamin-K intake alone
choices.explanation: These primarily relate to anticoagulant treatment.

choices.text: Oral lesions, fungal culture, and mouth-contact time alone
choices.explanation: These relate to local antifungal therapy.

questions.point: Monitor BP, fluid status, kidney function, and potassium.

questions.stem: After furosemide, urine output increases but the patient is more confused and hypotensive. Which conclusion is appropriate?

choices.text: Diuresis alone does not establish a safe beneficial response
choices.explanation: Perfusion, BP, renal function, and congestion must be reassessed.

choices.text: The dose should be repeated solely because urine increased
choices.explanation: A further dose requires review of the whole response.

choices.text: Confusion establishes that congestion has resolved
choices.explanation: It may reflect impaired perfusion or another problem.

choices.text: Higher urine output proves uncomplicated recovery
choices.explanation: The new hypotension and confusion are concerning.

questions.point: Evaluate breathing and edema, not urine volume alone.

questions.stem: A patient develops PVCs after several furosemide doses. Which mechanism best explains the lesson’s electrolyte concern?

choices.text: Direct AV dissociation is the intended loop effect
choices.explanation: The drug is not intended to produce heart block.

choices.text: Direct P2Y12 blockade is the defining loop effect
choices.explanation: Furosemide is not a P2Y12 antiplatelet.

choices.text: Increased potassium retention is the defining loop effect
choices.explanation: Loop diuretics are not potassium-sparing.

choices.text: Potassium and magnesium depletion can increase electrical irritability
choices.explanation: This connects diuresis with rhythm risk.

questions.point: New ectopy during diuresis can be electrolyte-related.

questions.stem: After furosemide, crackles improve but the patient develops postural dizziness, a BP fall, and rising creatinine. What interpretation best fits?

choices.text: The creatinine rise establishes that more fluid removal is always needed
choices.explanation: Renal deterioration requires context and an authorized review.

choices.text: Decongestion may coexist with excessive depletion and renal stress
choices.explanation: Benefit does not exclude treatment-related harm.

choices.text: Postural dizziness establishes recurrent pulmonary edema
choices.explanation: This does not explain the stated pattern.

choices.text: Improved crackles establish a safe volume status despite the other findings
choices.explanation: The hemodynamic and renal changes remain concerning.

questions.point: Excess diuresis can cause volume depletion, hypotension, and renal deterioration.

questions.stem: Which two clinical dimensions organize the lesson’s practical HF assessment?

choices.text: Platelet inhibition and clot dissolution
choices.explanation: These are drug mechanisms rather than HF assessment dimensions.

choices.text: Bowel obstruction and oral candidiasis
choices.explanation: These are different clinical problems.

choices.text: Congestion and poor perfusion
choices.explanation: Both may be present and require assessment.

choices.text: Drug absorption and tablet dissolution
choices.explanation: These do not describe the bedside HF pattern.

questions.point: Heart failure can involve congestion, inadequate output, or high filling pressures.

questions.stem: Which cluster most strongly supports congestion?

choices.text: Orthopnea, crackles, edema, and weight gain
choices.explanation: These are the taught fluid-backup findings.

choices.text: Dry mouth, urinary retention, and blurred vision
choices.explanation: These suggest an antimuscarinic effect.

choices.text: Nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech
choices.explanation: These suggest a different drug-toxicity pattern.

choices.text: Low urine output, cold skin, and confusion alone
choices.explanation: These primarily identify poor perfusion.

questions.point: Identify pulmonary/systemic congestion.

questions.stem: Which HF finding most directly suggests inadequate organ perfusion?

choices.text: Isolated peripheral edema without other changes
choices.explanation: Edema primarily suggests congestion.

choices.text: Isolated weight gain without other changes
choices.explanation: Weight gain primarily reflects a volume trend.

choices.text: Isolated raised JVP without other changes
choices.explanation: Raised venous pressure does not alone establish organ perfusion.

choices.text: New confusion with cold skin and oliguria
choices.explanation: This is a low-perfusion cluster.

questions.point: Identify poor perfusion in HF.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly describes the dominant backup patterns?

choices.text: Left: GI obstruction; right: urinary obstruction
choices.explanation: These are different organ problems.

choices.text: Left: platelet deficiency; right: clotting-factor deficiency
choices.explanation: These are not HF backup mechanisms.

choices.text: Left: pulmonary congestion; right: systemic venous congestion
choices.explanation: Lung and systemic venous findings are distinguished in the lesson.

choices.text: Left: systemic venous congestion only; right: pulmonary congestion only
choices.explanation: This reverses the principal patterns.

questions.point: Left and right ventricular failure produce different backup patterns.

questions.stem: What does left ventricular ejection fraction describe?

choices.text: The percentage of circulating platelets activated
choices.explanation: This is unrelated to ventricular ejection.

choices.text: The percentage of LV blood ejected with each contraction
choices.explanation: It is a fractional measure of systolic emptying.

choices.text: The percentage of blood oxygenated in the lungs
choices.explanation: That is not the definition of EF.

choices.text: The percentage of heartbeats conducted through the AV node
choices.explanation: EF does not measure AV conduction.

questions.point: EF describes the fraction of LV blood ejected, not the whole clinical severity.

questions.stem: A patient has a preserved EF but dyspnea and congestion with impaired ventricular filling. Which interpretation fits?

choices.text: A preserved EF proves all symptoms are noncardiac
choices.explanation: Other cardiac assessment remains necessary.

choices.text: A preserved EF excludes every HF diagnosis
choices.explanation: The lesson specifically distinguishes HFpEF.

choices.text: A preserved EF establishes normal filling pressures
choices.explanation: Filling abnormalities may coexist with preserved EF.

choices.text: HFpEF can occur with impaired filling despite preserved EF
choices.explanation: EF alone does not exclude HF or determine severity.

questions.point: Preserved EF does not exclude clinically important HF.

questions.stem: A patient has crackles and edema together with cold skin, hypotension, and confusion. Which classification best captures the bedside picture?

choices.text: Poorly perfused with congestion excluded
choices.explanation: Crackles and edema indicate a concurrent congestion concern.

choices.text: Both congested and poorly perfused
choices.explanation: The wet and cold patterns can coexist.

choices.text: Congested with adequate perfusion established
choices.explanation: The hypotension and confusion contradict that assurance.

choices.text: Neither congested nor poorly perfused
choices.explanation: Both sets of findings are present.

questions.point: Congestion and poor perfusion can coexist.

questions.stem: During HF observation, a patient develops sudden severe dyspnea and reduced consciousness. Which assessment has immediate priority?

questions.point: Osteomyelitis is bone infection with possible blood, contiguous, or direct entry.

questions.stem: Which cluster warrants consideration of deeper bone infection?

choices.text: A normal distal examination without wound symptoms
choices.explanation: This does not establish bone infection.

choices.text: A stable old scar without pain or drainage
choices.explanation: No active warning finding is described.

choices.text: A healed wound with steadily improving comfort
choices.explanation: This does not identify ongoing deeper infection.

choices.text: Persistent deep pain with drainage and poor healing
choices.explanation: This fits the lesson’s osteomyelitis warning pattern.

questions.point: Recognize persistent deep pain, drainage, poor healing, and inflammation.

questions.stem: Which set best supports a nursing report of suspected osteomyelitis deterioration?

choices.text: A tablet count without symptoms or observations
choices.explanation: Supply does not establish the clinical condition.

choices.text: A device photograph without a patient assessment
choices.explanation: Appearance alone is incomplete.

choices.text: Vitals, wound drainage, pain trend, and distal findings
choices.explanation: These establish local, systemic, and limb-safety information.

choices.text: A dressing brand and the original appointment date
choices.explanation: These do not describe current severity.

questions.point: Assess vitals, wound/drainage, pain trend, and neurovascular status.

questions.stem: Which treatment pattern is compatible with osteomyelitis in the lesson?

choices.text: A vitamin supplement as complete infection treatment
choices.explanation: Nutritional support does not replace antimicrobial/surgical care.

choices.text: A single analgesic dose as complete infection treatment
choices.explanation: Pain relief does not eradicate bone infection.

choices.text: A routine bronchodilator as complete infection treatment
choices.explanation: This does not treat a bone infection.

choices.text: An extended antimicrobial plan with possible debridement
choices.explanation: Both medical and surgical treatment may be required.

questions.point: Treatment may include prolonged antibiotics and surgery/debridement.

questions.stem: Which routes can lead to osteomyelitis in this lesson?

choices.text: Nearby infection only, without bloodstream or traumatic entry
choices.explanation: This excludes two taught routes.

choices.text: Bloodstream spread, nearby infection, direct traumatic entry
choices.explanation: These are the three taught routes.

choices.text: Bloodstream spread only, without local or traumatic entry
choices.explanation: This excludes two taught routes.

choices.text: Direct traumatic entry only, without bloodstream spread
choices.explanation: This excludes hematogenous and nearby spread.

questions.point: Bone infection may arise through bloodstream, contiguous spread, or direct inoculation.

questions.stem: A patient says a persistently draining wound is normal because it has drained for weeks. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: Chronicity does not make persistent drainage benign
choices.explanation: Deeper infection and poor healing still need assessment.

choices.text: Chronic drainage establishes eradication of infection
choices.explanation: Ongoing drainage does not establish cure.

choices.text: Absence of a new injury proves the drainage harmless
choices.explanation: Ongoing infection does not require a new injury.

choices.text: A long duration excludes bone involvement
choices.explanation: Persistent wounds and bone pain can support concern for deeper infection.

questions.point: Chronic drainage is not automatically normal.

questions.stem: A patient with a draining orthopaedic wound becomes febrile, hypotensive, and confused. Which response has priority?

choices.text: Complete the next planned education session first
choices.explanation: This delays assessment of acute systemic compromise.

choices.text: Treat drainage as the expected baseline without reassessment
choices.explanation: The systemic change invalidates that reassurance.

choices.text: Wait for the next elective wound review
choices.explanation: New instability requires earlier action.

choices.text: Assess ABCs/current observations and urgently escalate systemic deterioration
choices.explanation: The presentation may reflect a serious infection complication.

questions.point: Escalate systemic deterioration or worsening infection/hardware problems.
